strengths: The core idea of bypassing discrete tokenization for inter-model communication and exploring fully differentiable, continuous hidden-state interaction between language models is an interesting research direction.
The paper explores multiple applications, including scaling models and parameter-efficient adaptation across several standard benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, E2E).
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair experimental comparisons in Section 5.1: The authors compare LMNet-1B against purely pre-trained base models (e.g., Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B base, Llama-3.2-1B base) on benchmarks like GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU. However, LMNet-1B was explicitly trained on instruction-tuning data (Alpaca, LaMini, ProsocialDialog) and domain-specific training sets (GSM8K training split, MATH training split, MMLU auxiliary_training). Evaluating an instruction- and task-finetuned model against base models on the very benchmarks it was trained on invalidates the claims of superior performance.

Misleading compute and parameter claims: The paper claims to achieve comparable performance with 'less than 0.1% of the compute typically required to train a modern LLM from scratch' by training on 0.01T tokens. However, the backbone vertices are already initialized from Qwen2.5-0.5B (which was pre-trained on 18T tokens). Comparing continued fine-tuning on curated instruction/math data against pre-training from scratch on raw text is conceptually unsound.

Unaddressed inference cost and computational complexity: In LMNet-1B (a 5-layer topology with 1/4/4/4/1 vertices), each token generation requires passing through 14 full vertex forward passes (each being a 24-layer 0.5B transformer) plus 40 edge transformer layers. This amounts to ~376 transformer layers and over 7B parameters' worth of FLOPs per forward pass. Presenting LMNet-1B as a '1B-scale' model is deeply misleading because its runtime FLOPs, memory footprint, and latency are comparable to or worse than a 7B parameter model.

Discrepancy between concept and implementation: While the paper frames the method around 'Society of Mind', multi-agent collaboration, and collective intelligence, the practical implementation in Section 5 simply ties the weights of a single 0.5B model across all vertices and connects them with single-layer attention blocks. Functionally, this is equivalent to a deep recurrent/stacked transformer architecture with intermediate attention mixing, rather than true inter-model collective communication.

Trivial theoretical formulations: Proposition 1 ('End-to-End Gradient Descent') simply re-states standard backpropagation and the multivariate chain rule through composed neural network layers, presenting elementary calculus as a formal theoretical contribution.

Presentation and writing issues: There are unpolished sections and duplicate text; for example, on page 8 (Section 5.2.1), the exact sentence ('Second, these three LLMs are strong enough for such tasks with a single model given proper instructions, that the additional communication steps brought by LMNet does little help.') is repeated verbatim twice within the same paragraph. Furthermore, Appendix Figure 4 displays virtually identical, uninformative uniform green squares.

strengths: The core idea of replacing discrete token exchange with dense continuous vector representations between modular Transformer components is conceptually interesting and intuitively appealing for end-to-end differentiability.
The paper explores multiple use cases, including parameter-efficient adaptation on the E2E benchmark and modular model composition.
The parameter-sharing strategy across vertices keeps the total unique parameter count manageable.
weaknesses: Unfair and contaminated benchmark comparisons: In Section 5.1.1, LMNet-1B is trained on datasets that explicitly include the training splits of MMLU, GSM8K, and MATH, yet its performance is compared directly against raw pre-trained base models (e.g., Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B). Comparing a model fine-tuned on benchmark training data against base pre-trained models that have not undergone task-specific fine-tuning invalidates the claims of superior performance.

Misleading compute and token efficiency claims: The authors repeatedly claim that LMNet-1B achieves comparable performance to standard LLMs with 'less than 0.1% of the compute typically required' by training on only 0.01T tokens. This ignores the fact that the vertex modules are initialized from Qwen2.5-0.5B, which was already pre-trained on 18 trillion tokens. Adapting an existing heavily pre-trained checkpoint cannot be directly contrasted with training from scratch.

Conceptual overclaiming versus architectural reality: The manuscript frames the system in terms of 'collective intelligence', 'Society of Mind', and 'inter-agent communication'. However, the actual technical implementation is a parameter-shared, multi-branch Transformer network connected by single-layer attention modules. Framing standard differentiable layer stacking as multi-agent communication overstates the conceptual contribution.

Trivial theoretical presentation: Presenting standard backpropagation and the multi-layer chain rule as a formal theorem ('Proposition 1: End-to-End Gradient Descent') adds no theoretical depth and merely restates fundamental automatic differentiation.

Neglect of inference cost and latency: Autoregressive decoding through an LMNet with 5 layers and 11 total Transformer vertices incurs significant computational and memory bandwidth overhead. Even with intra-layer parallelization, generating tokens requires multiple sequential passes through the vertex models, making inference substantially slower and more FLOP-intensive than a monolithic 1B model.

Weak and unconvincing analysis: Section 5.1.2 attempts to inspect the learned communication, but notes that de-embedding the latent states yields nonsensical non-English output. Furthermore, Figure 4 in Appendix A consists of essentially identical uniform green blocks without meaningful quantitative or qualitative insight.

Draft quality and presentation issues: The paper contains numerous grammatical errors and awkward phrasing (e.g., 'many works combines', 'to for data-driven customization', 'that fuses a lot', 'This result in overfitting risk').

strengths: The paper explores continuous/dense vector interaction across neural modules, avoiding the discrete token generation bottleneck common in multi-agent workflows.
The proposed framework is evaluated across several distinct settings, including general language modeling/reasoning benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MATH) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning scenarios (E2E).
Weight sharing across vertexes is an interesting way to limit memory footprint while increasing the effective computational depth of the model.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons and data contamination: In Section 5.1.1, LMNet-1B is trained on Alpaca, LaMini, MMLU train split, MATH train split, and GSM8K train split, but is evaluated in Table 1 against base, pre-trained models (Qwen2.5 base, Llama-3.2 base, Gemma-2 base) that have not been instruction-tuned or trained on these task-specific datasets. Claiming superior performance with '< 0.1% training compute' is misleading when the training data includes supervised instruction and target-domain reasoning datasets.

Neglect of inference computational cost (FLOPs and latency): LMNet-1B comprises a 1/4/4/4/1 layer topology (14 vertex evaluations of Qwen2.5-0.5B plus edge attention blocks). While parameter count is kept at ~1.14B through weight sharing, the computational cost per forward pass is equivalent to a model with ~7B+ parameters. Comparing LMNet-1B strictly to ~1B parameter models without reporting inference FLOPs, wall-clock latency, and memory throughput obscures the true operational cost.

Conceptual framing vs. architectural reality: Framing this architecture as 'communication between LLMs' or 'collective intelligence' is largely metaphorical. Stripping embeddings and de-embeddings and connecting shared transformer blocks via 1-layer attention modules fundamentally constitutes a deep, looped/recurrent directed acyclic graph (DAG) transformer architecture. The paper does not provide comparisons against standard depth-scaled, recurrent, or MoE transformer architectures with equal inference compute.

Trivial theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 ('End-to-End Gradient Descent') states that composite functions of differentiable operations are differentiable via the chain rule. Presenting standard backpropagation as a formal proposition adds little technical value.

Inconclusive internal analysis and presentation quality: In Section 5.1.2, attempting to interpret intermediate states by de-embedding confirms they are arbitrary continuous latents rather than meaningful inter-agent communication. Figure 4 shows essentially indistinguishable, solid green heatmaps with unreadable labels. In addition, Section 5.2.1 contains duplicated sentences in the final paragraph.

strengths: Interesting conceptual exploration: The idea of connecting frozen or shared language model backbones into a differentiable DAG via intermediate seq2seq adapters to bypass discrete tokenization bottlenecks is intriguing and conceptually well-motivated.
Broad empirical coverage: The authors test across multiple benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP, E2E) and multiple model backbones (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2, GPT-2).

Candor regarding current limitations: Section 6.3 and Section 7 candidly discuss the fact that token-by-token autoregressive training does not yet realize true sentence-level agent communication and incurs substantial computational overhead.
weaknesses: Severe FLOPs and compute mismatch in baseline comparisons: The 1/4/4/4/1 LMNet topology executes 14 passes through the backbone model per generated token (totaling 336 transformer layers per token for Qwen2.5-0.5B, plus edge modules). Comparing this architecture against single-pass models (e.g., Qwen2.5-0.5B) without FLOPs- or latency-matched baselines is misleading. When compared against models with far fewer active parameters per token (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B in Table 7), LMNet is significantly outperformed on standard benchmarks (e.g., MMLU 53.9% vs. 60.9%; GSM8K 50.3% vs. 68.5%).

Conceptual disconnect between framing and reality: The manuscript motivates the method through multi-agent collaboration, 'Society of Mind', and agent workflows. However, because inference is strictly synchronous and token-by-token autoregressive, LMNet is essentially a wide, recurrent multi-branch transformer with shared weights and adapter layers. As acknowledged in Section 6.3 and Appendix B.2, intermediate representations do not form interpretable linguistic messages or agent-like communication, making the agentic framing somewhat disconnected from what is actually implemented.

Flawed baseline configurations and training setup: In Table 1, the SFT baseline degrades performance significantly across several benchmarks (e.g., MATH drops from 19.5% to 12.4%, BBH drops from 20.3% to 19.9%), suggesting severe optimization issues or catastrophic forgetting rather than a well-tuned baseline. Furthermore, on GSM8K (Table 9), when trained strictly on the task training set, LMNet underperforms prompt-based zero/few-shot baselines by large margins (30.93% vs. 41.60% on 0.5B; 60.02% vs. 68.50% on 1.5B), requiring the addition of 93.7k external OpenR1 data to surpass prompting.

Uninformative figures and presentation defects: Figures 4, 5, 6, and 7 consume three full pages in the appendix (pages 16–18) but consist entirely of tiny, solid green boxes with completely illegible text annotations. There are also noticeable typos and formatting issues (e.g., 'Figure 456 and 7' on page 13, missing URL placeholder on page 5, and awkward phrasing throughout).

strengths: Conceptual motivation: Exploring differentiable, dense-vector communication across reusable pre-trained language model nodes is an interesting direction to bridge discrete multi-agent frameworks and modular neural architectures.

Broad empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate across a diverse set of tasks (reasoning on GSM8K/MATH, general knowledge on MMLU/ARC, coding on HumanEval/MBPP, and generation on E2E) against several baselines including prompt engineering, SFT, test-time scaling (Self-Refine, Self-Consistency), latent reasoning (COCONUT, CODI), and PEFT methods.
Parameter-efficient design via weight sharing: By tying the vertex parameters across the network and only introducing 1-layer seq2seq edge modules, the static model footprint remains manageable.

Candid discussion of current limitations: In Section 6.3 and Section 7, the authors explicitly acknowledge that the current synchronous end-to-end autoregressive setup does not yet achieve true multi-step or sentence-level message passing between agents.
weaknesses: Disconnect between agentic framing and realized architecture: The paper heavily frames the work around multi-agent collaboration, collective intelligence, and bypassing discrete communication bottlenecks. However, because inference is synchronous and token-by-token end-to-end autoregressive, the architecture functions essentially as an ensemble of recurrent/parameter-tied transformer layers interleaved with shallow 1-layer attention blocks, rather than distinct communicative agents.

Unfair FLOP and inference cost comparisons: In the 1/4/4/4/1 topology, generating every single token requires 14 sequential/parallel passes through the 0.5B vertex backbone plus 16 edge module evaluations. Comparing this directly to single-pass models (e.g., Qwen2.5-0.5B prompt/SFT or 1B–3B monolithic LLMs in Table 7) without controlling for generation FLOPs or runtime latency is misleading, as the per-token inference computation of LMNet is comparable to a ~7B parameter model.

Lack of essential architectural baselines: Given that the vertex parameters are tied across layers, the model should be benchmarked against standard compute-matched and depth-matched baselines, such as looped/recurrent transformers (e.g., Universal Transformers), depth-scaled transformers, or Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.

Supervision efficiency claim is undermined on key benchmarks: On GSM8K under low-data supervision (Table 9), LMNet underperforms standard zero/few-shot prompting on both Qwen2.5-0.5B (30.93% vs. 41.60%) and Qwen2.5-1.5B (60.02% vs. 68.50%). The authors had to supplement the training with ~94k additional math problems from OpenR1-Math-220k (Table 3 and Table 8) to surpass prompting, which contradicts the core premise of supervision-efficient adaptation.

Inconclusive macro- and micro-level communication analysis: The parameter visualizations in Appendix B.1 (Figures 4–7) show uniform weight matrices without identifiable structure or role specialization across edges. Furthermore, the micro-level analysis in Appendix B.2 shows that intermediate inputs correspond to gibberish when projected back to vocabulary space, and intermediate outputs quickly collapse to the final answer rather than executing structured intermediate reasoning sub-steps.

strengths: Interesting conceptual exploration: The paper attempts to bridge the gap between multi-agent LLM systems and end-to-end differentiable neural architectures by proposing dense hidden-state communication between stripped transformer modules.
Comprehensive coverage of evaluation tasks: The authors evaluate the proposed method across a diverse set of standard benchmarks, including MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and E2E generation.

Transparent discussion of certain shortcomings: The authors honestly acknowledge in Section 6.3 and Section 7 that the current end-to-end token-level formulation does not actually achieve sentence-level agent communication and that intermediate activations do not de-embed into interpretable natural language.
weaknesses: Misleading conceptual framing vs. actual architecture: The manuscript frames LMNet as an agentic 'language model network' where models communicate and collaborate beyond discrete tokens. However, in practice (Section 3 and 6.3), LMNet is simply a branched, weight-shared deep transformer architecture where hidden states are processed auto-regressively token-by-token through 14 sequential/parallel transformer passes interleaved with 1-layer attention modules. Framing an expanded macro-transformer architecture as a multi-model agent network is a conceptual mismatch.

Unfair baseline comparisons and data contamination concerns: In Section 4.1 and Appendix A, LMNet is trained on a mixture that includes the training splits of MATH, GSM8K, and MMLU, yet it is compared against Prompt and TTS baselines that do not have supervised access to these training sets. Furthermore, the SFT baseline in Table 1 performs worse than prompting (-5.7% relative, dropping on MATH from 19.5% to 12.4%), which indicates an inadequately tuned baseline rather than an intrinsic advantage of the architecture.

Inadequate compute- and parameter-matched baselines: An LMNet with a 1/4/4/4/1 topology executes 14 full forward passes of a 0.5B model per generated token, totaling ~7B parameters worth of FLOPs per token. The paper does not compare LMNet against standard compute-matched architectures (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B) evaluated under identical training data budgets. Table 7 shows Qwen2.5-1.5B (which requires ~4.5x less FLOPs per token than 14x 0.5B passes) already outperforms LMNet on several key tasks (e.g., GSM8K: 68.5% vs 50.3%; ARC-C: 54.7% vs 38.0%).

Ablations contradict the core architectural hypothesis: In Table 6 (depth/width ablation on E2E), increasing the network capacity and width (e.g., 1/4/1 and 1/4/4/1) actually degrades performance compared to a narrower 1/2/1 setup (BLEU drops from 70.5 to 69.1 and 68.7). This contradicts the claim that a dense, layer-wise fully connected MLP-like topology provides superior expressiveness and scalability.

Uninformative edge analysis: The visualization in Appendix B.1 and Figures 4–7 shows uniform, featureless weight matrices across all edges with no distinguishable structure or sparsity pattern. Along with the observation that intermediate vertex representations rapidly collapse to redundant outputs (Figure 3), there is little evidence that the complex graph topology learns specialized collaborative communication protocols.
